name: Maya Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Maya, and thank you for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the big front-end loader on the ore pad at the zinc mine, feeding the primary crusher, and I lead the crusher crew on my shift. If I get the blend wrong, the mill upstairs has a bad day, so it's a job where you have to think. I've been the lead for six years and I train all the new loader operators. I love it when the crusher runs smooth for a whole shift and nobody's on the radio. What wears me out is that the crusher crew gets paid less than the pit crews, even though we work the same hours.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Tom is an electrician, self-employed, so some months are good and some are thin. Our son's sixteen and talking about university, our daughter's twelve. We have a mortgage on a house near the church, and honestly not much in the bank, less than a month. Sundays are church and lunch at my mother's, that's not negotiable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, the sky didn't fall. I'd say it at the Sunday lunch, and my brother-in-law who's always reading about AI would have to eat his words. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not hugely, because I didn't think the AI was coming for my loader anyway. I use the chatbot now and then for the church newsletter, and it's handy. If that's all it ever is, fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do. I'd keep putting money aside for my son's university, even if it's only twenty a week. And I'd ask the supervisor again about bringing crusher pay up to pit pay, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you didn't think AI was coming for your loader. Has anything changed on the pad already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a sensor system now that tells me the ore grade in each pile, so I blend better. When it came, I waited to see if it was right, and after a few weeks it was. Now I wouldn't want to go back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you ask politely about the pay, rather than pushing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I think you get further being reliable than being loud. My dad always said, do the work and they'll notice. They haven't noticed in six years, mind, so maybe he was wrong about that one.

S0.say: I'd say the sky didn't fall and make my AI-obsessed brother-in-law eat his words at Sunday lunch. I'm not one for posting online.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved but not hugely, since I never thought AI was after my loader. I use the chatbot now and then for the church newsletter, and that's fine if it's all it ever is.
S0.do: Keeps working as usual and sets aside about twenty a week for her son's university. Asks her supervisor again, politely, about lifting crusher pay to match the pit.
S0.quote: They haven't noticed in six years, mind, so maybe he was wrong about that one.
S0.fieldNote: Maya values reliability over protest, a lesson from her father that she half questions. She adopted the grade sensor only after it proved itself. Her son's university fund is her quiet priority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to roll up their sleeves and learn the new ways, and companies should train their own people rather than lay them off. I'd say the community should look after its own through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the loader goes autonomous in a few years, like the trucks at some mines. Somebody would still need to watch the blend and the crusher, and I'd want that to be me. It depends on whether they value experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen it working at another site, I'd ask to train on the control side early. I'd cut back on eating out and the cable, maybe fifty a month, and keep the university fund going. And Tom would look at getting certified for the mine's automation wiring, since electricians would be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a way through, but I'd want to see it before I trusted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the community looking after its own. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The church has a job board in the hall, and people help each other with lifts and meals when there's trouble. When the sawmill closed ten years ago, that's how families got through. I'd expect the same, and I'd do my part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your son's university plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still want him to go, but I'd ask him to think about what he studies. Something practical, engineering maybe. He wants to do history, and I'd be lying if I said that doesn't worry me.

S1.say: I'd say people need to roll up their sleeves and learn new ways, and companies should train their own staff rather than lay them off. The community should look after its own through it.
S1.think: I really think the loader goes autonomous in a few years, though someone will still need to watch the blend and crusher. I'd want that to be me, if they value experience.
S1.do: Asks to train on the control side once she has seen it work at another site. Cuts eating out and cable by about fifty a month, keeps the university fund going, and Tom looks at certifying for automation wiring.
S1.feel: Uneasy, wanting to see the path before trusting it.
S1.quote: He wants to do history, and I'd be lying if I said that doesn't worry me.
S1.fieldNote: Maya trusts community and church networks, citing how families survived the sawmill closure. She'd retrain, but only after seeing the new system work elsewhere. Her son's choice of study is where her worry lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too much too fast, and nobody voted for it. I'm not one for big government, but someone has to slow this down. And I'd say families need to stick together, because that's what will get us through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the loader and the crusher control both go within a year or two, and Tom's work dries up too if robots do wiring. We'd have no savings and two incomes gone. I'd be scared stiff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Tom the first night and work out what we can live on. We'd stop the university fund and use it for the mortgage, which would break my heart. I'd ask my mother about moving in with her if we had to, and I'd go to the church job board on the first Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray a lot, and I'd still be awake at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said stopping the university fund would break your heart. Why that one first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a house is a roof for four people and university is a hope for one. That's how I'd have to think, even though he's my son. He'd understand, I think, he's a good boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother, my sister and the church, in that order. Not the government, unless there was no choice. If there was nothing else, I'd take it, I suppose, for the kids.

S2.say: I'd say it's too much too fast and nobody voted for it, and that someone has to slow it down even though I'm not one for big government. Families need to stick together to get through.
S2.think: I think the loader and crusher control both go within a year or two, and Tom's wiring work dries up too. With no savings and both incomes gone, I'd be scared stiff.
S2.do: Works out a bare-bones budget with Tom on the first night and diverts the university fund to the mortgage. Asks her mother about moving in and checks the church job board on the first Sunday.
S2.feel: Alarmed: praying a lot and awake at three in the morning.
S2.quote: Because a house is a roof for four people and university is a hope for one.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI threatens both incomes in Maya's home at once. She would turn first to family and church, and accept government help only as a last resort for her children. Choosing the mortgage over her son's fund was clearly painful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some years, so let's use them: apprenticeships, retraining, companies keeping their loyal people. I'd want the mine to tell us the plan so we can plan our families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get a few years on the control side if I train for it. Tom could get into automation wiring and ride that a while. The university fund might survive, which matters to me a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the control-room training in the first year or two, once the first group had shown it works. Tom would do the automation certificate. We'd keep the university fund going and try to build a month's savings by year three, which we've never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do with my hands, so to speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying once others have shown it works. What would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone like me, a loader operator, sitting in that room a year later and not hating it. I don't need the company brochure, I need to talk to her at the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change what you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son engineering, not history, and I'd say it more firmly. My daughter's twelve, she loves animals and the church choir. I'd let her be twelve for now.

S3.say: I'd say there are some years, so let's use them for apprenticeships, retraining and keeping loyal staff. I'd want the mine to share its plan so families can plan.
S3.think: I think I'd get a few years on the control side if I trained, and Tom could ride automation wiring for a while. The university fund might survive, which matters to me a lot.
S3.do: Takes control-room training within the first year or two after others prove it works, while Tom does an automation certificate. Keeps the university fund going and aims for a month's savings by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, with practical things to do.
S3.quote: I don't need the company brochure, I need to talk to her at the canteen.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Maya returns to her pattern of following once someone she trusts has shown the way. Both she and her husband plan to retrain. She becomes firmer about steering her son towards engineering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and good families and good companies will use it well. I'd tell the young ones at church to pick a trade that'll last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years is manageable for us. My son would be through university, my daughter nearly, and I'd be fifty-three with some years left on the control side or in something else. It'd still be hard, but it wouldn't break us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train on the control side when others had shown it works, maybe in year two or three. We'd keep the university fund going and slowly build two months of savings. And I might help run a skills night at the church hall, if the company would send someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but at peace with it mostly. God gives us time for a reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten years that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the company waits until the last minute to tell us. They did that with the mill shutdown last year, told us two weeks before. Ten years only helps if they're honest early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the end of those ten years to look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both kids settled, mortgage nearly paid, and me still working somewhere I'm useful. Maybe training people, I'm good at that. And still Sunday lunch at my mother's, if she's with us.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning, and good families and good companies will use it well. I'd tell young people at church to choose a trade that lasts.
S4.think: I think ten years is manageable: my son through university, my daughter nearly, and me at fifty-three with some working years left. It would be hard, but it wouldn't break us.
S4.do: Trains on the control side in year two or three once others have shown it works. Keeps the university fund going, slowly builds two months of savings, and helps run a skills night at the church hall.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly at peace, seeing the time as given for a reason.
S4.quote: Ten years only helps if they're honest early.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lines up with Maya's family timeline and her faith, so she feels mostly at peace. Her doubt is about the company's honesty, after a mill shutdown announced at two weeks' notice. She pictures herself training others.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Tom and I could lose work at the same time and my son's university would go first. What would help is the company keeping people on while they retrain, and honest notice, years not weeks, so families can plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women on the crusher crew. There are four of us now, and we fought to get there. I'd want to know we're kept on for the new jobs, not just the men who shout loudest.

headlineQuote: My dad always said, do the work and they'll notice.
portrait: Maya Garcia is a 43-year-old loader operator and crusher crew lead at a zinc mine, married to a self-employed electrician, with a teenage son hoping for university, a younger daughter, a mortgage and less than a month saved. She is a churchgoer who prefers being reliable to being loud, and she adopts new technology once she has seen it work. She is content if AI stalls and uneasy under steady change, then alarmed by fast AGI because both household incomes and her son's university fund are at risk. With more time she plans to retrain after others prove the way, leaning on family and church rather than government.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her husband could lose work at the same time and her son's university fund would go first.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping people on while they retrain, and honest notice measured in years rather than weeks.
